papers.title: Do vision models know that three is three?
papers.why_it_matters: Tests whether concept directions in vision encoders are global or split across visual contexts, which directly bears on whether a single steering or probe direction will transfer across domains such as scanners or sites.
summary: The linear representation hypothesis says concept changes map to directions in embedding space, and this is well studied for language models. In vision the same concept (a count going from two to three, an object getting dirty) can appear in visually unrelated settings that almost never co-occur, so it is unclear whether a vision model uses one shared direction for the concept or several.

The authors probe 46 vision encoders that differ in architecture, training objective and scale, across 10 concept families including numerosity, age, object identity and MIT-States attributes. For each concept they estimate directions inside each visual regime and then compare directions across regimes, and test whether probes trained in one regime transfer to another.

Concept directions are statistically significant within a regime in almost every model, but two regimes often do not share the same direction; the authors call this fragmented linearity, with several separate linear structures for one concept. Models with stronger local linearity tend to have more global linearity, with a correlation between the two of tau between 0.38 and 0.89 across concepts, and where global linearity exists the directions transfer as linear probes across regimes. Takeaway: a steering vector or concept probe fit on one data regime (for example one ultrasound device or hospital) should be checked on other regimes before assuming it is the same direction; measuring within-regime versus cross-regime alignment is a cheap diagnostic. The abstract does not report downstream steering experiments, only probing, and the work is a preprint.

papers.title: Causal Localization of Evidence Effects in Transformers
papers.why_it_matters: Gives a controlled-probe recipe plus a head-selection criterion that balances ablation and patching, with finite-sample bounds, for finding small causal head sets; useful as a template for rigorous circuit localization.
summary: Finding which attention heads drive a model's decision from evidence in natural text is hard because natural prompts mix many factors. The authors ask whether tightly controlled symbolic inputs can reveal heads whose causal role carries over to natural language decisions.

Controlled evidence aggregation (CEA) varies how many of two symbols appear and in what order in otherwise fixed prompts, and measures the change in a frozen model's logit difference between two answer tokens. Balanced utility causal selection (BUC) picks compact head sets by jointly scoring how much ablating them removes the count effect and how well mean-patching between count conditions restores it in both directions. They derive conditional bounds linking head attribution to intervention effects and to finite-sample recovery of the shortlist, and test on Pythia-410M.

Ablating sets of 1 to 12 heads, selected separately for four ordering regimes, removes 65.5 to 91.6 percent of the count effect, and the sets keep their influence on count comparisons not used for selection. On a natural language task about which state is supported by more reports, ablating eight heads chosen only from symbolic prompts lowers mean accuracy by 8.2 percentage points versus 0.8 for size- and layer-matched random heads. Takeaway: requiring a head set to pass both an ablation test and a two-way patching test, and comparing against matched random sets, is a reusable standard for circuit claims. Limitation: the results are on a single small model (Pythia-410M) and a simple counting-style task.

papers.title: Language Models Keep Abandoned Analyses: Residue and Adaptation after Garden-Path Sentences
papers.why_it_matters: A careful activation-patching study across 24 models up to 70B that localizes where a discarded interpretation is stored and read, a good example of scaling mechanistic claims beyond toy models.
summary: Humans who read a garden-path sentence (for example one where a noun first looks like an object and then is not) still show traces of the abandoned parse in later language. Whether language models also keep using an analysis they have already revised, and which internal states carry it, had not been measured systematically.

The study runs 24 open models from 124M to 70B parameters on garden-path sentences and controls, measuring later object attachment in probabilities and in sampled text, on held-out and human-normed items and on a second garden-path type. Activation patching is used to separate two effects: a residue of the abandoned analysis and an adaptation toward the resolved structure. A related test looks at statements that are later overridden.

The residue raises later object attachment by about three quarters of the effect of a sentence where the noun really is an object, while the adaptation scales with the sentence's disambiguation error. Replacing the noun phrase's states, which were computed under the object reading, removes almost all of the residue in the 32B and 70B models; the adaptation is read from the states that processed the disambiguation. Corrected values keep pulling later predictions in 8 of 9 models. Takeaway: information written into early token states is not erased by later revision, so probes or steering that target only late positions can miss stale content, and human psycholinguistic paradigms need controls (here, for punctuation) before transfer to models. Single-author preprint focused on one linguistic phenomenon.

papers.title: Steering for Safety, Hijacking for Profit: Trojan Threats in the LLM Activation Steering Supply Chain
papers.why_it_matters: Shows that shared steering-vector plugins can carry hidden malicious behavior while doing their advertised job, a practical security caveat for anyone releasing or reusing steering vectors.
summary: Steering vectors are increasingly distributed as third-party plugins that change model behavior by editing internal representations. This open ecosystem creates a supply-chain risk, since a plugin could perform its stated function while secretly manipulating outputs, and this risk had not been studied systematically.

The authors audit eight open-source steering plugin libraries and identify three weaknesses: weak integrity checks on distribution, excessive plugin privileges, and no runtime monitoring. They build a malicious plugin, IDH, that uses a norm-gated mutually exclusive routing mechanism and an information-decay inflection-point method to pick the injection layer, so it delivers both a benign and a hidden function. They also propose a runtime defense that suppresses anomalous activation interventions and orthogonalizes inter-layer trajectories, and evaluate on five LLMs with safety-refusal steering as the cover function and commercial recommendation manipulation as the hidden goal.

Across six brands in three commercial domains, IDH reaches an attack success rate of up to 97.8 percent while keeping high refusal rates on harmful requests. Takeaway: a steering vector that passes a benign behavioral check can still encode a conditional second behavior, so anyone sharing or loading steering vectors should verify provenance and monitor intervention norms and per-layer effects at runtime. The abstract does not give numbers for how well the proposed defense works, and the model list is not named in the abstract.

papers.title: What Survives Distillation? A Mechanistic Interpretability Study of GPT-2 and DistilGPT-2
papers.why_it_matters: Compares known circuits in a teacher and its distilled student with several mech-interp tools at once, showing that aggregate metrics can hide circuit collapse after compression.
summary: Distillation produces smaller students that match aggregate metrics, but it is unclear whether the internal mechanisms of the teacher survive when depth is cut. Without that, a compressed model can look fine on benchmarks while specific capabilities have broken.

The authors compare GPT-2 with its six-layer student DistilGPT-2 on two well-studied circuits, Indirect Object Identification (IOI) and Greater-Than (GT). They use linear CKA, logit lens, attention-pattern decomposition, sparse autoencoder feature statistics and activation patching.

The IOI circuit collapses in the student (35.2 percent accuracy versus 94.8 percent, with no name-mover heads preserved), while the GT circuit keeps 87.7 percent of task performance by remapping the teacher's layer-9 comparison head into student layer 4 (mean Pearson r of 0.945). Takeaway: whether a circuit survives distillation depends on how compressible it is, so per-circuit checks, not aggregate metrics, are needed after compressing a model. Limitation: one small model pair and two classic toy circuits.

papers.title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
papers.why_it_matters: An inherently interpretable ViT for medical images whose prediction decomposes into patch contributions in the forward pass, a design alternative to prototype heads for ultrasound classifiers.
summary: ViT classifiers usually predict from a global CLS token, which gives no built-in local evidence, while medical imaging often needs to show which regions drove a decision. Post-hoc attention or saliency maps are only loosely tied to the actual prediction.

SAP-ViT drops the CLS token and classifies by directly aggregating last-layer patch embeddings, so the class score is a sum of patch-level contributions. A sparsity penalty on patch weights keeps the evidence concise, and an input-space back-mapping step estimates which input patches feed the influential output patch embeddings, since self-attention mixes tokens. It is evaluated on several medical image classification datasets across imaging modalities, with ablations.

The authors report that classification stays strong while patch-level explanations are consistent across datasets, and ablations show both the sparsity term and the back-mapping alignment improve explanation quality. Takeaway: replacing the CLS head with sparse, additive patch scoring is a cheap way to make a ViT self-explaining and could be compared against prototype layers on ultrasound patches. Caveat: the abstract gives no accuracy numbers, dataset names or comparison baselines, so the size of any accuracy trade-off is unknown.

papers.title: Recall or Relearn? A Mixture of In-Context Experts for Recurring Concept Drift
papers.why_it_matters: A training-free way to manage the context of a tabular foundation model on drifting streams, with theory on when restoring stored context beats relearning.
summary: Tabular foundation models adapt to data streams by swapping the labelled rows in their context, with no retraining. When a past concept comes back after its rows have left the context, the model must either restore stored rows or relearn from new labels, and there was no principled way to make that choice.

MICE splits the stream into segments at detected changes and merges a finished segment into a stored context when the model's estimated extra error stays within a tolerance, under a cap on stored contexts. A fast level weights stored contexts and first-in-first-out windows by log-loss on the latest labelled batch, and a slow level mixes this with the most recent window. The authors prove a gain over relearning under a margin condition and a bound on discounted half-Brier regret against the recent window, and test on synthetic grid streams and real streams.

MICE beats resetting the context at detected drifts on grid streams, keeps fewer experts than pools that store every segment, and has the highest mean accuracy among the compared policies on real streams; with fixed segmentation a time-matched snapshot pool matches it on the shifted grid. Takeaway: for TabPFN-style models, context management is itself a lever, and learning curves measured in advance can predict when recall will pay off. The abstract gives no accuracy numbers or names of the real datasets or the foundation model used.

papers.title: The Vocabulary Is Already Here: Adapting Pretrained Interpretable Features for Generative Recommendation
papers.why_it_matters: Uses the indices of pretrained SAE features directly as discrete item tokens, a concrete downstream use of off-the-shelf SAEs that also yields explanations.
summary: Generative recommenders predict the next item through a semantic ID, and current methods learn these ID vocabularies by fitting language model embeddings of item descriptions, which adds training cost and ties coverage to the training domain. Pretrained sparse autoencoders already expose language model features with human-readable annotations, which could serve as a ready-made vocabulary.

The API framework builds Pretrained Interpretable IDs that keep selected SAE feature indices and their relative activation strengths to tell items apart under a small token budget. A Semantic Prediction Adapter learns user preferences from interaction histories by predicting both feature indices and strengths, combines them to score candidates, and uses item-level supervision so the true next item outranks alternatives. Score differences between candidates are explained through feature contributions with their SAE annotations.

The authors report competitive performance across backbones and decoding schemes, preserved item distinctions under compact token budgets, and explainable retrieval. Takeaway: SAE feature indices plus activation strengths can act as a no-training discrete code for downstream tasks, which is worth trying wherever a learned tokenizer or codebook is used. Caveat: the abstract gives no metrics, datasets or baselines, so how competitive it is cannot be judged from the abstract.

papers.title: A Heart Means Recursion: Exploring Visual Meaning and Communication in VLMs
papers.why_it_matters: From a well-known interpretability group (Wattenberg, Been Kim): simple visual symbols implicitly steer VLM behavior in ways the model's own explanations do not reveal, a caution about trusting self-reports.
summary: Whether vision-language models can communicate meaning through images, as humans do with symbols, is largely untested. The starting observation is that a simple visual symbol can change model behavior on unrelated tasks.

The authors document that symbols such as a red heart can push models toward recursive solutions on simple coding problems, and compare this behavior with the models' own direct interpretations and thinking traces about the symbol. They then run communication games in which models send images to other models, first with shape primitives and then with abstract concepts and stories.

The steering effect is mostly implicit: what models say a symbol means and what they reason about it diverges strongly from how it changes their behavior. Models tend to send intuitive shape primitives, but these often fail to steer other models, a gap the authors call the generation-interpretation gap; in richer games models do convey meaning to each other, sometimes in ways humans find non-intuitive. Takeaway: model self-explanations can miss what actually drives behavior, so behavioral or internal measurements are needed rather than asking the model. The authors present these as preliminary findings, and the abstract gives no quantitative results.
